deep.reconstruction:
Context (from p.266): Two nearby surfaces I and II carry equal and opposite amounts of (magnetic) fluid, i.e. a double layer or magnetic shell. Its surface is z = z(x,y), and the ω are the elements of its projection III onto the xy-plane. The constant factor ε i k ζ collects the strength and thickness of the layer, the current intensity and similar constants.

On p.266 Gauss writes the force components contributed by one element pair as
∂X ω = (εikζ ω / r^5) { 3xy z_x + (3y^2 − r^2) z_y − 3yz },
∂Y ω = −(εikζ ω / r^5) { (3x^2 − r^2) z_x + 3xy z_y − 3xz },
Z ω = 0,
with r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2.

Comparison with the dipole field (my check) identifies these. The element has normal moment ∝ (−z_x, −z_y, 1) ω, and its field at the origin is B. Then ∂Y = B_x, ∂X = −B_y and Z = 0. So (X, Y, Z) ∝ e_z × B: the force on a current element directed along the z-axis at the origin. Equivalently, by reaction, it is the shell–current-element interaction.

Still on p.266, Gauss rewrites the X-integrand, using 3y^2 − r^2 = 2r^2 − 3x^2 − 3z^2, as an exact plane divergence:
X ω = εikζ ω [ ∂_x( x z_y / r^3 ) − ∂_y( (x z_x − z) / r^3 ) ].
Here ∂_x, ∂_y are total derivatives with z = z(x,y); the mixed terms x z_xy cancel.

This page:
1. He singles out the two pieces εikζ dy (∂_x P) dx with P = x z_y / r^3, and εikζ dx (∂_y Q) dy with Q = (x z_x − z) / r^3.
2. For the first, he cuts the projection III into infinitely thin strips parallel to the x-axis. Each strip integrates to the boundary difference [P]_left^right dy.
3. For the second, he uses strips parallel to the y-axis, giving [Q]_bottom^top dx.
4. Summing ('daraus folgt sehr leicht') yields Green's theorem in the plane: ∬_III (∂_x P − ∂_y Q) dx dy = ∮_∂III (P dy + Q dx).
5. Along the boundary curve, dz = z_x dx + z_y dy (implicit step, mine). Hence P dy + Q dx = (x z_y dy + x z_x dx − z dx)/r^3 = (x dz − z dx)/r^3.
6. So ΣXω = εikζ ∮ (x dz − z dx)/r^3 = εikζ ∮ (x dz/ds − z dx/ds)/r^3 ds, taken around the whole perimeter. Gauss traverses the perimeter so that III lies to the right.
7. In the same way, ΣYω = εikζ ∮ (y dz − z dy)/r^3. The underlying identity, which I verified, is: −[(3x^2 − r^2) z_x + 3xy z_y − 3xz]/r^5 = ∂_x((y z_y − z)/r^3) − ∂_y(y z_x / r^3).
8. These are exactly the components (up to the e_z × rotation) of the Biot–Savart/Laplace field ∮ (r × ds)/r^3 of a current flowing along the boundary curve.

Conclusion: the shell bounded by a closed curve acts like a closed current along that curve. Combined with his §§194–195, Gauss declares 'das Ampère'sche Gesetz' proved, i.e. Ampère's equivalence of a closed current and a magnetic shell. The surface integral depends only on the boundary.
errors: No algebraic error: the divergence identity for X (p.266) and the analogous one for Y both check out exactly, with the second-derivative terms cancelling.

Orientation: with the usual axes (x right, y up), the strip argument gives ∮(P dy + Q dx) with the region on the LEFT (counterclockwise). Gauss says the perimeter is traversed so that III lies on the RIGHT. Either he uses the opposite orientation convention for the xy-plane (or for the direction of the current or normal), or there is a sign slip. This cannot be decided from this page alone.

The strip argument tacitly assumes each line parallel to an axis meets the boundary of III in two points (convex or simply decomposable region), and that the surface is a graph z(x,y) over III. This is standard but unstated.
The step from the strip boundary differences to the single line integral (using dz = z_x dx + z_y dy on the boundary) is left implicit ('sehr leicht').

results.what: Force (field) of a magnetic double layer over a surface z=z(x,y) written as an exact plane divergence and reduced to a contour integral ∮(x dz − z dx)/r^3, ∮(y dz − z dy)/r^3 over its boundary
results.modern_name: Ampère's equivalence theorem (magnetic shell ≡ closed current), proved via Green's theorem in the plane (a Stokes-theorem computation for a graph surface)
results.usually_credited_to: Ampère (1820–1826, Théorie mathématique des phénomènes électrodynamiques); the general integral theorem to Green (1828)/Kelvin–Stokes (1850/1854)

results.what: Strip decomposition of a planar region to convert ∬(∂P/∂x − ∂Q/∂y)dxdy into a boundary integral
results.usually_credited_to: Green 1828 / Cauchy, Ostrogradsky; special cases known earlier (including Gauss 1813 for the divergence theorem)

results.what: Line-integral expression of the force of a closed current on a current element/pole at the origin
results.modern_name: Biot–Savart–Laplace law (integrated over a closed loop)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, correct derivation of Ampère's shell–current equivalence via a Stokes/Green-type reduction for a graph surface. Ampère himself had essentially this transformation (1826). Gauss's electrodynamic notes of the 1830s with Weber (Werke V) show he worked on exactly such questions, and he had used surface-to-boundary integral theorems since 1813. The neat exact-divergence form is a nice unpublished detail, but not a priority-changing result.

transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'dy' is struck through and 'dx' follows, i.e. εikζ.dx.(∂(x(dz/dy)/r^3)/∂x .dx); the transcription's [-dy-] is right.
Second display opens with a curly brace and closes with a round parenthesis; this is Gauss's own inconsistency, faithfully kept.
In the Y-formula on the right, the 'dy/ds' has the y written over another letter (likely a corrected x), so ∂y/ds is the intended reading.
Left-hand denominators in both final formulas are r^3 (the second looks like 'r3' and could be misread as 'r1').
